What Bad Coaching Looks Like in Personal Growth (And Why It Is More Common Than People Realise)

What Bad Coaching Looks Like in Personal Growth (And Why It Is More Common Than People Realise)

29 May

What Bad Coaching Looks Like in Personal Growth (And Why It Is More Common Than People Realise)

The coaching industry has grown into a multi-billion-dollar market around the world, and the quality of what gets delivered varies enormously. Most clients have no reliable way to distinguish coaching that builds genuine capacity from coaching that simply feels productive. 

Bad coaching for personal growth often looks attentive, purposeful, and well-structured, right up until it stops working. So how can you spot the signs?

1. The Coach Who Has the Answer Before You Do

One of the clearest signs of a bad coach is the use of questions to lead a client toward a conclusion the coach has already reached. The technique can look like a skilled inquiry. The client feels heard, the session feels alive, and the insight feels earned.

But if the destination was always the coach’s, the client hasn’t actually developed anything. They’ve been guided to someone else’s thinking. When coaching steers rather than explores, the client gradually learns to trust the coach’s judgment over their own. This creates a quiet dependency. Clients return session after session because outside thinking feels more reliable than internal reflection, and that reliability was never actually challenged.

Genuine coaching holds the question open long enough for the client to find their own meaning. That’s uncomfortable for everyone. It’s also what growth actually requires.

2. The Coach Who Fixes Instead of Develops

The fixing pattern is seductive. A client names a problem. The coach identifies a solution. Progress appears to happen.

What this misses is that in personal growth, the visible problem is rarely the whole story. The behavior someone struggles with, the decision they keep deferring, the habit that keeps returning: these are almost always symptoms of a deeper structure. A set of assumptions about who they are, what they’re capable of, what they deserve. Coaching that resolves the surface issue without touching what sits beneath it tends to produce short-term relief and long-term recurrence.

The work can look effective for months. Goals get ticked off. The client reports wins. The deeper structure stays exactly where it was.

3. The Coach Who Makes It About Progress, Not the Person

Performance-oriented coaching, structured around goal tracking, action steps, and accountability, is not inherently negative coaching. But when that structure becomes the whole of the engagement, something important gets left out.

Personal growth doesn’t always move in a straight line. The most significant shifts often happen in the pauses, in the contradictions, in the moments when a client sits with something they don’t yet understand. 

A coaching relationship organized entirely around output can replicate the pressure a client is already living under, rather than creating space for something new to emerge. The irony is that slowing down is often more productive than accelerating. In a culture that rewards visible momentum, that’s a difficult case to make, and a rare coaching behavior to encounter.

What to Look for in a Coaching Relationship That Actually Works

Good coaching is easier to feel than to describe, but the markers are consistent. The coach listens for what sits beneath the words, not just the content of the problem. The client’s own thinking is treated as the primary material, not something to be corrected or redirected.

Over time, a client in a genuinely developmental coaching relationship should notice:

  • Growing capacity to sit with ambiguity without immediately reaching for an answer

  • Clearer access to their own values and reasoning, independent of the coach

  • Fewer repetitions of the same core challenges under different surface conditions

  • A sense of expanding agency, not increasing reliance on external guidance

Effective coaching is measured by one thing over time: whether the client becomes progressively less dependent on the coach to navigate their own life.

The Distinction That Changes Everything

The quality of a coaching relationship determines whether a person develops new capacity or cycles through the same challenges with better vocabulary. That is not a small distinction.

Recognizing what bad coaching looks like, and understanding what makes a bad coach, is part of developing the discernment to find something better.
